questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State Newton's second law of motion. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to show the relationship between force (F) and acceleration (a). Your description should include:

- a list of apparatus needed
- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use to collect data
- how the data will be used to show the relationship between force and acceleration
- any precaution taken to minimize error. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The rate of change of momentum of a body is **directly proportional to the resultant force** acting on it and takes place **in the direction of the force**. For a constant mass this gives $F = ma$: the acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass.

(ii) **Apparatus:** a trolley, a runway (a long smooth board that can be tilted), a pulley fixed at the end of the runway, string, a hanger with slotted masses (for example ten $10\,\mathrm{g}$ masses), a ticker-timer with its tape and power supply (or two light gates and a timer), a metre rule and a mass balance.

**Diagram of the set-up (described):** the runway lies on the bench with the ticker-timer fixed at its upper end. The trolley is on the runway, with a ticker tape fastened to its back and passing through the timer. A string from the front of the trolley passes over the pulley at the lower end of the runway and carries the hanger with the slotted masses, which pull the trolley.

**Procedure:**

1. Tilt the runway slightly until the trolley, given a small push, runs down at constant speed (the tape shows equally spaced dots): this compensates for friction.
2. Put all the slotted masses (total mass $m$) on the trolley, so that the total mass of trolley plus slotted masses stays constant during the experiment. Take one mass off the trolley and hang it on the hanger. The pulling force is $F = mg$ of the hanging masses.
3. Release the trolley from rest and let it pull the tape through the timer.
4. From the tape, find two velocities: $v = \dfrac{\text{distance of a chosen set of dots}}{\text{time of that set}}$, then the acceleration $a = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{t}$, $t$ being the time between the two sets of dots (or read $a$ from the timer when using light gates).
5. Repeat for $F$ = 1 weight, 2 weights, 3 weights ... by moving one more mass each time from the trolley to the hanger, and record $F$ and $a$ in a table.

**Use of the data:** plot a graph of acceleration $a$ (y-axis) against force $F$ (x-axis). A **straight line through the origin** shows that $a$ is **directly proportional to $F$** (for constant mass); its gradient is $1/M$, where $M$ is the total mass moved.

**Precautions:** compensate for friction by tilting the runway; keep the total mass constant by transferring (not adding) masses; keep the string parallel to the runway; release the trolley from rest each time; stop the trolley at the end of the runway (cushion) so that it does not fall; repeat each reading and take the mean.

questions.enonce_markdown:
An object weighing 500 N on earth is taken from the earth's surface to another planet whose acceleration due to gravity is $6.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(i) Give one difference between mass and weight. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Calculate the weight of the object on this planet. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Mass** is the quantity of matter in the object (a scalar, measured in kg) and does not change with place; **weight** is the gravitational force acting on the object (a vector, measured in newtons) and **varies with the strength of gravity**.

(ii) On earth, $W = mg$, so $m = \dfrac{500}{10} = 50\,\mathrm{kg}$.

The mass is the same on the other planet, so

$W = m g' = 50\times6.5 = 325\,\mathrm{N}$.

**The weight on the planet is $325\,\mathrm{N}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A uniform metre bar of length $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ and mass $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ is pivoted at its $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark. A load, X, is placed at the end of the bar closer to the pivot to balance the weight of the bar.

(i) Define the moment of a force. *[1 mark]*

(ii) State two conditions necessary for an object to be in equilibrium. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Draw a diagram showing all the forces acting on the bar and their respective distances from the pivot. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Calculate the weight of the load, X. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The moment of a force about a point is the **product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the point (pivot) to the line of action of the force**, $M = F\times d$ (unit: N m).

(ii) (1) The **resultant force** on the object is zero (the sum of the forces in one direction equals the sum in the opposite direction). (2) The **resultant moment** about any point is zero (the sum of the clockwise moments equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments).

(iii) **Diagram (described):** a horizontal bar from the $0\,\mathrm{cm}$ end to the $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ end, pivoted at the $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark.

- The load X acts **downwards** at the $0\,\mathrm{cm}$ end, $30\,\mathrm{cm}$ ($0.30\,\mathrm{m}$) from the pivot.
- The weight of the bar, $W = 20\times10 = 200\,\mathrm{N}$, acts **downwards** at its centre, the $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark, $20\,\mathrm{cm}$ ($0.20\,\mathrm{m}$) from the pivot, on the other side of the pivot.
- The reaction $R$ of the pivot acts **upwards** at the pivot, $R = X + 200$.

(iv) The bar is uniform, so its weight acts at its centre, at the $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark. Taking moments about the pivot:

$X\times0.30 = 200\times0.20$

$X = \dfrac{40}{0.30} = 133.3\,\mathrm{N}$.

**The weight of the load is about $133\,\mathrm{N}$** (a mass of about $13.3\,\mathrm{kg}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define specific heat capacity. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block. Your description should include:

- a list of apparatus needed
- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure you will use to collect data
- how the data will be used to obtain the specific heat capacity
- any precaution taken to minimize error. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The specific heat capacity of a substance is the **quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of the substance by $1\,\mathrm{K}$ (or $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)**. Unit: $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

(ii) **Electrical method.**

**Apparatus:** an aluminium block (about $1\,\mathrm{kg}$) with two holes drilled in it, an electric immersion heater, a thermometer, a low-voltage d.c. supply (for example 12 V), an ammeter, a voltmeter, a switch, connecting wires, a stopwatch, a mass balance, lagging (felt or cotton wool) and a little oil.

**Diagram of the set-up (described):** the block stands on an insulating mat and is wrapped in lagging. The heater is in one hole and the thermometer in the other, each with a drop of oil for good thermal contact. The heater is connected in series with the ammeter, the switch and the supply, and the voltmeter is connected across the heater.

**Procedure:**

1. Measure the mass $m$ of the block with the balance.
2. Read the initial temperature $\theta_1$ of the block.
3. Switch on the supply and start the stopwatch at the same time; note the voltmeter reading $V$ and the ammeter reading $I$ (keep them constant).
4. After a time $t$ (for example 10 minutes) switch off and note the highest temperature $\theta_2$ reached by the thermometer.

**Use of the data:** electrical energy supplied $E = VIt$, and it raises the temperature of the block, $E = mc\,(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$. Hence

$c = \dfrac{VIt}{m\,(\theta_2 - \theta_1)}$.

**Precautions:** lag the block to reduce heat losses to the surroundings; put oil in the holes so that the heater and the thermometer are in good thermal contact with the metal; read the highest temperature reached after switching off (the temperature keeps rising for a short time); keep the current and voltage constant; repeat and take the mean.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mass of $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water is heated with a $500\,\mathrm{W}$ heater for 20 minutes.

(i) Calculate the heat supplied by the heater supplied during this time. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Given that the specific heat capacity of water is $4200\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, determine the change in temperature of the water during this time. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Explain why water is often used as a cooling liquid in car radiators. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Time $t = 20\times60 = 1200\,\mathrm{s}$.

$Q = Pt = 500\times1200 = 600\,000\,\mathrm{J} = 6.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$.

**The heat supplied is $6.0\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$.**

(ii) $Q = mc\,\Delta\theta$, so

$\Delta\theta = \dfrac{Q}{mc} = \dfrac{600\,000}{5\times4200} = 28.6\,\mathrm{K}$ (assuming no heat loss).

**The temperature rises by about $28.6\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($28.6\,\mathrm{K}$).**

(iii) Water has a **high specific heat capacity**, so it can absorb a large quantity of heat from the engine for a small rise in its own temperature and carry it away to the radiator, where it is released to the air. (Water is also cheap, easily available and flows easily.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student used an un-calibrated thermometer in the laboratory to measure the temperature of a given liquid. He first put it in pure melting ice and the mercury thread was $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ long. He then removed it and put in steam from boiling water, the mercury thread was $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ long. Then he puts it in the liquid and the mercury thread was $35\,\mathrm{cm}$ long.

(i) Define temperature. *[1 mark]*

(ii) State two properties that make mercury suitable for use in thermometers. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Calculate the temperature of the liquid. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Temperature is the **degree of hotness or coldness of a body**, a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles; it decides the direction in which heat flows.

(ii) Any two of: it **expands uniformly (regularly)** with temperature; it is a **good conductor of heat**, so it responds quickly; it is **opaque and shiny**, so it is easy to see; it **does not wet (stick to) the glass**; it has a **wide liquid range** (freezing point $-39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, boiling point $357\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

(iii) The lower fixed point ($0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) corresponds to $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the upper fixed point ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) to $50\,\mathrm{cm}$, a length of $40\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$\theta = \dfrac{35 - 10}{50 - 10}\times100 = \dfrac{25}{40}\times100 = 62.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

**The temperature of the liquid is $62.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.**
